title: The God who hears the cry
hookLine: hear both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor
carry: god hears two cries: the earth's and the poor's

lines: ONE PAIR OF EARS, TWO CRIES.
cards: A burning bush in the desert, and a voice from inside it. Moses, a shepherd on the run, hears God say, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have seen the affliction of my people in Egypt, and I have heard their cry."
Before the plagues, before the sea, before any rescue, there's a God who listens. In Laudato Si', Pope Francis takes that act of hearing and doubles it.
A true ecological approach, he says, must become a social approach, one that hears both the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor. Two cries. One pair of ears.

teach.b: First, the cry of the poor. A psalm in the Douay-Rheims puts it simply: "This poor man cried, and the Lord heard him." In the Catholic tradition, that cry has a claim on everyone who hears it.

teach.h: THE CRY OF THE EARTH: CREATION GROANS.
teach.b: Second, the cry of the earth. That sounds stranger. Can soil cry?
Paul thinks creation itself has a voice. Writing to the Romans, he says: "For we know that every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now." Groaning, like a woman in labor.
Francis picks up that language. He describes the earth as among the most abandoned and mistreated of the poor, burdened and laid waste. Third, why they belong together.
When a forest is cleared, the families who lived from it are rarely the ones who profit from the timber. When land dries out, it's often the poorest farmers who can't move or adapt.

teach.h: HEAR ONE, AND YOU MISHEAR THE OTHER.
teach.b: So if you listen to only one cry, you'll mishear the other. An environmental plan that ignores the poor can end up pushing them aside. A plan for the poor that ignores the land can end up stripping what they live on.
At the burning bush, God hears first, then acts.
The order holds here too: listen, then respond. Not with despair, and not by trying to fix the whole world before lunch. With one real response, where you are.

how: Catholic groups that work on Laudato Si' often pair environmental projects with service to the poor, and some parishes and religious communities hold prayer services built around the cry of the earth and the cry of the poor.

o: the shepherds' alarm calls in the Psalms
the earth's cry and the poor's, heard together
two prayers said at dawn and again at dusk

p: a claim on everyone who hears it

s: Francis counts the earth itself among the poor
he describes it as among the most abandoned and mistreated of the poor, burdened and laid waste.
"every creature groaneth and travaileth in pain, even till now."
in the burning bush, God acts first and listens later
God says: I have seen, I have heard their cry. hearing comes first.

games.q: you have one free afternoon. a food bank needs hands, and so does a creek cleanup. what does today's teaching on two cries ask of you?
o: research for weeks until you find the biggest cause.
do nothing until you can answer both.
hear both, then make one real response where you are.
games.why: hearing comes first, then one real response. not despair, and not fixing the whole world before lunch.

practice: Let the cry of the poor come to mind, a person or a place you know is struggling, and stay with it a moment.
Then let the cry of the earth come, a field paved over, a dirty creek, a summer that was too hot, and choose one of the two to answer with one small response: a donation, a call, a cleanup, a meal.
If you pray, bring both cries to God; if you don't, simply let yourself hear them.

wordCard.voice: Two cries. The cry of the earth and the cry of the poor, which Francis says must be heard together. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: God hears two cries, the earth's and the poor's. One pair of ears is enough to start. See you tomorrow.
